nameStory: The painted-tongue gets its artistic name from its spectacular flowers that look like they've been hand-painted with intricate brushstrokes and patterns. The blooms feature bold veining and color combinations that resemble an artist's palette, while the flower's shape vaguely suggests a tongue or trumpet.
description: Painted-tongue is a stunning annual flower originally from Chile that's grown as a garden ornamental in New England. It produces large, funnel-shaped blooms in vibrant colors like purple, yellow, red, and orange, often with intricate veining and patterns that make each flower look hand-painted. The plants typically grow 1-3 feet tall with somewhat sticky, lance-shaped leaves and an upright branching habit.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large funnel or trumpet-shaped blooms 2-3 inches across with velvety petals featuring intricate veining patterns in contrasting colors - often purple with gold veins or yellow with dark purple markings

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly sticky or clammy to the touch, with a somewhat bitter smell when crushed - arranged alternately on the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant 1-3 feet tall with branching stems that may need staking in windy locations

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small capsules containing tiny dark seeds, typical of the nightshade family

habitat: In New England, painted-tongue is found exclusively in cultivated gardens, containers, and flower beds as an ornamental annual. It prefers well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade and is not naturalized in wild areas.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are typically started indoors in late winter or sown directly in gardens after the last frost. Young plants begin establishing with their characteristic sticky leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with continuous production of showy flowers from early summer through fall if deadheaded regularly. This is when identification is easiest.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until first hard frost, with seed capsules developing and maturing. Plants become more ragged-looking as season progresses.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely with frost, leaving only seeds. No above-ground parts persist through New England winters.

funFact: The leaves of painted-tongue are so intensely bitter that its Spanish name 'palito amargo' literally means 'bitter little stick' - the bitterness is so extreme it can make your mouth pucker just from a tiny taste!
confusionNotes: Painted-tongue might be confused with petunias from a distance, but petunias have smoother, less sticky leaves and lack the intricate painted veining patterns. The velvety texture and complex color patterns of painted-tongue flowers are distinctive once you look closely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, painted-tongue belongs to the nightshade family along with tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes. Like many of its relatives, it contains compounds that make it unpalatable to most animals, which explains the extreme bitterness of its leaves.
compareHints: Painted-tongue is the only species in its genus found in New England gardens. Within the nightshade family, it's most similar to petunias but distinguished by its intensely bitter, sticky leaves and the characteristic intricate veining patterns on its velvety flowers. Unlike the solid or simple-patterned petunias, painted-tongue flowers look genuinely hand-painted with complex designs.
